Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection $\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]], [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give $m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so $m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure $m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures, and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them on the entire Borel sigma-algebra ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on $\mathbb T^n$ ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],

$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

For the given rectangle, fix once for all inputs and support sets an affine copy of the bump in
[A1] on each side interval. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of
rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than
every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. By [F1] its continuous compact-interval integral exists; positivity makes it nonzero, so
normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. The primitive
difference quotient differs from $h(x)$ by at most $\sup\{|h(s)-h(x)|:s\text{ lies between }x\text{
and }x+\delta\}$, which tends to zero by continuity. Its derivative is therefore $h$, and it
vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its
support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the
zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$.

Here and below the coordinate integrals of smooth compactly supported functions may be computed
on the closed coordinate intervals after extension by zero. This extension is smooth on a
neighborhood of the closed box: compact support leaves a neighborhood of every boundary face where
the function is zero. By [F1] the function and every coordinate section are Riemann integrable;
[F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box
integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal
to $\int_\Omega h$.

To differentiate a marginal, fix all other coordinates and restrict the differentiated
coordinate to a compact interval inside its open side interval. The integrand and each parameter
derivative are continuous on the resulting compact two-variable rectangle, so repeated [F3] gives
$$\partial_{x'}^\beta H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}\partial_{x'}^\beta h(s,x')\,ds,\qquad \sup|\partial^\beta H|\le (b_1-a_1)\sup|\partial_{x'}^\beta h|.$$
The inequality follows from [F4] with the second integrand zero. Continuity of these derivatives
jointly in the remaining parameters follows from the same bound applied to their differences and
uniform continuity of the integrand derivative on each compact box.

The same reasoning differentiates an integral with upper endpoint $x_1$ in its other parameters.
For its $x_1$ derivative, the difference quotient of $\int_{a_1}^{x_1}f(s,x')\,ds$ differs from
$f(x_1,x')$ by at most $\sup_{s\text{ between }x_1\text{ and }x_1+\delta}|f(s,x')-f(x_1,x')|$, which
tends to zero by continuity; higher endpoint derivatives then follow by ordinary differentiation.
This proves the finite-integral identities used in the recursion.

For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. By step 1.2, $\int

$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$
Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes

Assume full AC. Let $d\ge2$, $R>0$, and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)\subset(-R,R)^d$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. The two conclusions therefore justify the distinction stated in the Remark. No step extends the rectangle argument to arbitrary bounded open sets or strengthens $H^{-1}$ to $L^2$; either extension would need an additional proved right-inverse or inf-sup estimate.
